reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: A severe viral haemorrhagic fever caused by filoviruses (Ebolavirus), with fruit bats implicated as the likely reservoir and human outbreaks often seeded by contact with infected wildlife or bushmeat
Human-to-human spread occurs through direct contact with blood or body fluids of symptomatic patients and with contaminated surfaces, and corpses remain highly infectious
Illness begins abruptly with fever, profound malaise, myalgia, and headache, followed by prominent gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and profuse diarrhoea causing major fluid losses
Overt haemorrhage occurs in a minority, and much of the mortality is driven by volume depletion, electrolyte disturbance, and shock rather than bleeding alone
High-quality supportive care with aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement substantially improves survival, and specific monoclonal antibody therapies are now available
This is a public health emergency demanding strict isolation, full personal protective equipment, safe and dignified burial practices, and immediate notification to authorities
Prevention includes vaccination of contacts and at-risk groups (ring vaccination) and rigorous infection-prevention measures in healthcare settings
reference.pathophysiology: Ebolaviruses are enveloped RNA filoviruses that infect a broad range of cells, including macrophages, dendritic cells, and endothelium, while actively suppressing interferon-based innate immunity. Widespread viral replication drives a massive dysregulated inflammatory and cytokine response, impaired coagulation with disseminated intravascular coagulation, and increased vascular permeability. The combination of capillary leak, huge gastrointestinal fluid losses, and coagulopathy produces intravascular volume depletion, shock, and multi-organ failure, which underlie the high mortality.
additionalDifferentials: Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Lassa, Marburg, CCHF)
infectionMimics: Marburg and other viral haemorrhagic fevers
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR for Ebola viral RNA as the primary diagnostic test, performed under maximal biosafety
Antigen detection and serology (IgM/IgG) where appropriate
Malaria testing and other investigations to exclude common endemic causes, done with strict precautions
Electrolytes, renal and liver function, and coagulation studies to guide supportive care
All specimen collection and transport coordinated with designated laboratories and public health authorities
redFlags: Profuse vomiting and diarrhoea with signs of severe volume depletion and shock
Bleeding, bruising, or laboratory evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation
Confusion, agitation, or other neurological deterioration
Any suspected case is a public health emergency requiring immediate isolation, full PPE, and notification, given the extreme transmission risk
reference.prognosis: Untreated Ebola virus disease has historically carried very high case-fatality, but early presentation, intensive supportive care, and specific antibody therapies markedly improve survival; convalescence can be prolonged and survivors may experience persistent symptoms and viral persistence in immune-privileged sites.
pitfalls: Failing to isolate and don appropriate PPE promptly, risking healthcare-associated outbreaks
Under-resuscitating patients by focusing on bleeding while overlooking massive gastrointestinal fluid losses
Attributing illness solely to malaria or typhoid in an outbreak or travel context and delaying containment
Neglecting safe burial practices and contact tracing, which are central to outbreak control
management: Give specific monoclonal antibody therapy (ansuvimab or the atoltivimab-maftivimab-odesivimab combination) early to improve survival
Deliver aggressive oral and intravenous fluid resuscitation with electrolyte replacement to counter gastrointestinal losses and hypovolaemic shock, the core of survival
Provide symptomatic care with antiemetics, antipyretics and analgesia and nutritional support, correcting coagulopathy and supporting failing organs
Treat concurrent malaria and secondary bacterial infection empirically given endemic co-infection
Institute strict isolation, full personal protective equipment and safe, dignified burial practices to prevent transmission
Notify public health authorities immediately, coordinate specimen handling under maximal biosafety, and undertake contact tracing with ring vaccination of contacts
Arrange survivor follow-up for persistent sequelae and viral persistence in immune-privileged sites such as the eye, central nervous system and semen
